=== PUC-59142-Opposition-Letter-Broussard.pdf ===
               BEFORE THE PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION OF TEXAS

                                  PROJECT NO. 59142

      REVIEW OF ERCOT'S INTERCONNECTION PROCESSES FOR LARGE LOADS

      PUBLIC COMMENT IN OPPOSITION TO SYNERGEN GREEN ENERGY, INC.'S
                       REQUEST FOR GOOD CAUSE EXCEPTION

To the Commissioners of the Public Utility Commission of Texas:

I am submitting this public comment in opposition to Synergen Green Energy,
Inc.'s September 11, 2026 request for a good cause exception to ERCOT's Batch
Zero eligibility deadlines. I respectfully urge the Commission to deny the request.

My name is Roger D Broussard. I live in Calhoun County, Texas, where Synergen
wants to build its ammonia plant. I am a concerned resident, not a party to this
proceeding, and I am not asking to intervene. I am writing because this decision
affects my county, my neighbors, and the rules every developer is supposed to live
by.

1. The deadlines were known.

ERCOT published a schedule for Batch Zero: a readiness kickoff on May 15, 2026,
implementation documents in early June, and deadlines of July 10 and July 24, 2026.
That was not a secret process. And by Synergen's own account, the company had
been working with South Texas Electric Cooperative on this project since July 2024,
contracted for a load study and system impact study in August 2025 at a cost of
$200,000, and received its steady state report in April 2026. Yet by its own account,
Synergen did not sit down with STEC to discuss the new Batch Zero rules in any
detail until July 7, 2026, three days before the first deadline. A company that had
two years to prepare does not get to call a published deadline a surprise.

2. The money argument cuts the other way.

Synergen says it has spent $30.5 million and cannot afford to lose it. But the
financial security it failed to post was $15 million, less than half of what it says it has
already spent. A company that can spend $30.5 million on a project can post $15
million in security for it. That money was spent as a business decision, and it does
not buy an exception. If investment alone were good cause, then the rules would
 apply only to companies too small to matter, and every large developer could buy
its way past any deadline.

3. An exception here means exceptions for everyone.

ERCOT has said it received forty-one good cause exception requests. If the
Commission grants this one, it tells every other developer that deadlines are
optional when the stakes are high enough. That is not how a fair process works.
The Batch Zero rules were written to be applied the same way to everyone, and the
Commission should apply them that way here.

4. A 300-megawatt load in a rural county deserves real answers first.

Synergen's plant would draw about 300 megawatts in a rural area. Before the
Commission advances this project through interconnection, it should have
documented answers: what new transmission lines and substations will be needed,
what they will cost, and who will pay for them. Synergen points to about 890
megawatts of wind and solar under contract, but a power purchase agreement is
not the same as firm power. The wind does not always blow and the sun does not
always shine, and the plant will need power when neither is producing. Those are
questions for the record, not assurances to take on faith.

5. Our community's concerns deserve weight.

Calhoun County residents have real concerns about this project: the scale of its
electricity demand, its use of groundwater, air quality, wastewater, industrial
safety, and the future of our communities. I am not opposed to responsible
industrial development. I am opposed to special treatment for one developer
because it promises jobs and tax revenue. And I ask the Commission to make clear
that granting an interconnection exception would not be approval of this facility,
which still needs its permits from the agencies that govern water, air, and safety.

For these reasons, I respectfully request that the Commission deny Synergen
Green Energy's request for a good cause exception, require Synergen to show
specific, documented grounds if it seeks any relief, and preserve the Batch Zero
process as it was written, the same rules for everyone.

Thank you for considering these comments.

Respectfully submitted,
 Roger D Broussard

Calhoun County, Texas

November 18, 2026
